q: What is an Apex trigger?
alt: Can you explain what a trigger is in Salesforce?
what is a trigger in apex
Why do we use triggers in Salesforce?
Tell me about Apex triggers in simple words
a: An Apex trigger is Apex code that runs automatically before or after records are inserted, updated, deleted or undeleted on an object. A trigger is defined on one object, lists the events it listens to, and receives the affected records through context variables like Trigger.new. For example, a trigger on Opportunity can listen for after update, and when a deal moves to Closed Won, it creates an onboarding Case for that account. We use triggers when declarative tools like Flow can't handle the logic cleanly, for example complex cross-object validation, heavy bulk processing with maps, or logic that needs tight control over errors and recursion. As a best practice, I keep the trigger itself very thin and put the real logic in a handler class.
points: Runs automatically on DML: insert, update, delete, undelete
Before or after the record is saved
Records come in through context variables like Trigger.new
Keep the trigger thin, logic in a handler class

q: What are the different trigger events in Salesforce?
alt: How many trigger events are there?
List the events a trigger can run on
Is there a before undelete trigger?
what are trigger events before insert after insert etc
a: There are seven trigger events: before insert, before update, before delete, after insert, after update, after delete and after undelete. There's no before undelete. Before events are for validating or changing the records being saved, without any extra DML. After events are for when you need the record Id or you're working with other records, like creating children or updating a parent. For example, defaulting a Lead's Rating as it's saved is before insert. Creating a follow-up Task for a new Contact needs the Contact's Id, so that's after insert. One trigger can list several events, and I normally list all the events an object needs in a single trigger and route them to a handler.
points: 7 events: before/after insert, update, delete, plus after undelete
No before undelete event
Before: change or validate same records; after: related records, Ids

q: What are trigger context variables?
alt: Explain Trigger.new, Trigger.old, newMap and oldMap
What context variables are available in a trigger?
what is trigger dot new and trigger dot old
What does Trigger.isExecuting mean?
a: Context variables tell the trigger what's happening and give it the records. Trigger.new is the list of new versions of the records, and Trigger.old is the list of old versions. Trigger.newMap and Trigger.oldMap hold the same records keyed by Id. Boolean flags like isInsert, isUpdate, isDelete, isUndelete, isBefore and isAfter tell you the event and timing. Trigger.operationType gives the event as a single enum value, Trigger.size gives the number of records in this invocation, and Trigger.isExecuting is true when the current code was called from a trigger. The combination I use most is in an update: I take a record from Trigger.new, look up the same Id in Trigger.oldMap, and compare them to see whether, say, the Stage actually changed.
points: Trigger.new / Trigger.old: lists of records
Trigger.newMap / Trigger.oldMap: maps keyed by Id
isInsert, isUpdate, isDelete, isUndelete, isBefore, isAfter
operationType, size, isExecuting

q: What is the difference between a before trigger and an after trigger?
alt: Before vs after trigger, when do you use which?
When should I write a before trigger instead of an after trigger?
before trigger versus after trigger difference
Why can't I update Trigger.new in an after trigger?
a: I use a before trigger when I want to validate or change the same records that are being saved, because I just set fields on Trigger.new and Salesforce saves them, with no extra DML. For example, filling in a default region on a new Account is a before insert job. I use an after trigger when I need the record Id or the saved values, or when I'm working on other records, like creating child records, updating a parent, or enqueuing a Queueable. In an after trigger, Trigger.new is read-only. So changing the same record there would need another update statement, which wastes limits and can cause recursion. That's why same-record changes belong in before.
points: Before: same-record field updates and validation, no DML needed
After: record Ids available, related records, async jobs
Trigger.new is read-only in after triggers

q: Which trigger context variables are available in which events?
alt: Is Trigger.newMap available in before insert?
Why is Trigger.new null in a delete trigger?
In which events can I use Trigger.oldMap?
when is trigger new map not available
a: Trigger.new is available in insert, update and undelete triggers, and you can only modify it in before triggers. Trigger.old is available in update and delete triggers. Trigger.newMap is available in before update, after insert, after update and after undelete, but not in before insert, because new records don't have Ids yet. Trigger.oldMap is available in update and delete triggers. So in a delete trigger I work with Trigger.old or oldMap. For example, to stop someone deleting an Account that still has open Cases, my before delete logic loops over Trigger.old, because Trigger.new isn't available there. And in before insert, I only have Trigger.new as a list.
points: Trigger.new: insert, update, undelete (editable only in before)
Trigger.old and oldMap: update and delete
Trigger.newMap: not in before insert (no Ids yet)
Delete triggers: use Trigger.old

q: Why do you get a 'Record is read-only' error in an after trigger, and how do you fix it?
alt: I'm getting FinalException record is read-only in my trigger
Can we update Trigger.new in after insert?
how to fix record is read only error apex trigger
Why can't I set a field on Trigger.new in after update?
a: That error appears when you try to change a field on a record in Trigger.new inside an after trigger. In after context the records are already saved, so Trigger.new is read-only. Say an after insert trigger on Case tries to set a Status on the same Case. That line throws the error. The fix is to move that field assignment into the before trigger, where you set the value directly and it's saved with no extra DML. If you really need the after context, for example because the value depends on the record Id, then build new sObject instances with just the Id and the changed field, and update those, with a guard so the update doesn't loop.
points: After trigger records are read-only
Move same-record changes to before trigger
If after context is needed, update new instances by Id with a guard

q: What is bulkification in triggers and why is it important?
alt: How do you make a trigger bulk safe?
What does it mean to bulkify a trigger?
Why should a trigger handle 200 records at a time?
bulkify apex trigger example
a: Bulkification means writing the trigger so it works correctly and efficiently when it receives up to 200 records at once, not just one. Data Loader, integrations and batch jobs send records in bulk, and governor limits apply to the whole transaction. So a query or DML per record quickly hits the 100 SOQL or 150 DML limit. For example, if someone loads 200 Contacts and my trigger queries the parent Account once per Contact, that's 200 queries, and the load fails. The pattern I follow is: loop once to collect Ids into a Set, run one query into a Map, loop again to apply the logic, collect the changes into a List, and do a single DML at the end.
points: Trigger can receive up to 200 records per invocation
Collect Ids in a Set, query once into a Map
No SOQL or DML inside loops
One DML on a list at the end

q: How do you avoid SOQL and DML inside a for loop in a trigger?
alt: Show me a trigger with SOQL in a loop and fix it
How do you remove queries from inside loops?
my trigger has update inside for loop how to fix
Rewrite this trigger so it doesn't hit too many SOQL queries
a: I move every query and DML out of the loop. First I loop through the trigger records and collect the Ids I need into a Set. Then I run one query with WHERE Id IN :set, or a parent-to-child query, and store the results in a Map or list. Then I loop again, make the changes in memory, add the records to a List, and do one update at the end. In this example, when an account owner changes, all open opportunities move to the new owner with one query and one DML, no matter how many accounts are in the batch.
points: Bad: query or update per record
Good: collect Ids, one query, one DML
Only process records whose field actually changed

q: Why should you have only one trigger per object?
alt: What is the one trigger per object pattern?
What happens if there are two triggers on the same object?
why one trigger per object best practice
Should I create a new trigger for every requirement?
a: Because if there are multiple triggers on the same object for the same event, Salesforce doesn't guarantee which one runs first, so the behaviour is unpredictable and hard to debug. Say one trigger sets an Account's region, and a second trigger assigns the owner based on that region. If the second one happens to run first, it reads a blank region and assigns the wrong owner. With one trigger per object, I control the order of logic explicitly inside the handler. I can apply a single recursion strategy and a single bypass switch, and every developer knows exactly where to look. The trigger just delegates to a handler class, and the logic is split into well-named methods or service classes that are easy to unit test.
points: Order of multiple triggers on the same event isn't guaranteed
Single entry point controls order explicitly
One place for bypass and recursion logic
Thin trigger, logic in handler and service classes

q: Can you write a trigger handler framework?
alt: How do you structure a trigger with a handler class?
Show me your trigger framework
explain trigger handler pattern with code
What does a base trigger handler class look like?
a: Sure. I keep the trigger to one line that calls the handler's run method. A base class does the routing with a switch on Trigger.operationType, checks a bypass list, and has an empty virtual method for each event. Each object handler extends the base class and only overrides the events it needs, calling service classes for the real logic. For example, my AccountTriggerHandler only overrides beforeInsert, to default the Rating, and afterUpdate, to move open opportunities when the owner changes. The other events just do nothing. This gives one trigger per object, a predictable order, one place for bypass logic, and handler methods I can unit test. Teams can also bypass a handler from code through a static bypass set, for example during a data fix.
points: Trigger calls handler.run() only
Base class routes events with switch on Trigger.operationType
Object handler overrides only needed events
Static bypass set to switch handlers off in code

q: How do you use Trigger.operationType in a trigger?
alt: What is System.TriggerOperation?
Use switch on in a trigger instead of if else
how does trigger operation type switch work
What values does Trigger.operationType return?
a: Trigger.operationType returns a System.TriggerOperation enum, like BEFORE_INSERT or AFTER_UPDATE, which combines timing and event in one value. I use it with a switch on statement instead of nested if conditions on isBefore and isInsert. It reads cleanly, every event is routed in one place, and one when branch can cover several events. For example, if before insert and before update both need to default the same field, I write one when branch listing BEFORE_INSERT and BEFORE_UPDATE and call the method once. The values are BEFORE_INSERT, BEFORE_UPDATE, BEFORE_DELETE, AFTER_INSERT, AFTER_UPDATE, AFTER_DELETE and AFTER_UNDELETE.
points: Returns System.TriggerOperation enum
Use with switch on for clean routing
One when branch can list several values

q: How do you prevent recursion in a trigger?
alt: How do you stop a trigger from firing again and again?
What is the best way to handle recursive triggers?
trigger recursion static set of ids
My trigger is calling itself, how do I stop it?
a: I use a static Set of Ids in the handler to remember which records have already been processed in this transaction. Static variables live for the whole transaction, so when my after update logic does a DML that fires the same trigger again, the records already in the set are skipped. For example, an after update on Account updates a field on those same Accounts. That update fires the trigger again, but those Ids are already in the set, so the logic doesn't run twice. I prefer this over a static Boolean, because a Boolean blocks every later chunk of 200 records and any legitimate second update. I also check that the relevant field actually changed using oldMap, which on its own stops most recursion.
points: Static Set<Id> of processed records, not a static Boolean
Statics live for the whole transaction
Also check real field changes with oldMap
Boolean guard skips later 200-record chunks

q: Your recursion check uses a static Boolean, and when 1,000 records are inserted in one Apex DML only the first 200 get processed. Why?
alt: Why is a static boolean a bad way to stop recursion?
Trigger logic only ran for the first 200 records, what is wrong?
static boolean run once trigger problem
Records after the first chunk were skipped by my trigger
a: Because a static Boolean is shared across the whole transaction, and a single DML of 1,000 records fires the trigger in chunks of 200 within that same transaction. The first chunk sets the flag to true, so the next four chunks see it and skip the logic. The same thing happens when another automation legitimately updates the record again in the same transaction. The fix is to track processed record Ids in a static Set, so each record is handled once but new records are still processed, and to only run logic when the relevant fields changed.
points: Trigger runs per 200-record chunk in the same transaction
Boolean set by chunk 1 blocks chunks 2 onwards
Use static Set<Id> plus field-change checks

q: How do you decide between a trigger and a record-triggered flow?
alt: Flow vs trigger, which one would you use?
When would you choose Apex trigger over Flow?
trigger or flow how to decide
Should all automation move to Flow?
a: My default is Flow for simple same-record updates and straightforward automation, because admins can maintain it, and before-save flows are very fast for field updates. For example, setting a Case's priority from its type is a perfect before-save flow. I choose a trigger when the logic is complex or needs heavy bulk processing with maps, precise error handling, reusable Apex services, async callouts, or events Flow doesn't support, like undelete. I also follow a per-object rule. Mixing many flows and triggers on one object makes the order of execution hard to reason about, so a team should agree which tool owns which object.
points: Flow: simple, admin-maintainable, before-save is fast
Trigger: complex logic, large volumes, fine error control
Record-triggered flows have no undelete event
Agree a per-object standard to avoid mixing

q: How do you use addError in a trigger?
alt: How do you show a validation error from a trigger?
What is the difference between record addError and field addError?
how to stop a record from saving in trigger
Throw a custom error message on a field from Apex
a: addError stops the record from being saved and shows a message to the user. If I call it on the record, the message appears at the top of the page. If I call it on a field, like contact.Email.addError, it shows next to that field. For example, if the business wants only work email addresses on Contacts and someone enters a personal one, I put the error right on the Email field so the user sees exactly what to fix. In an all-or-none DML the whole operation fails, while with partial success only the records with errors fail. I mostly call it in before triggers for validation, and I keep it bulk-safe by checking all records in one loop, without querying per record.
points: record.addError: message at top of page
record.Field.addError: message next to the field
Use in before triggers for validation
All-or-none DML fails all; partial success fails only bad records

q: Can you use addError in an after trigger, and what happens?
alt: Does addError work in after insert?
Can I block a save from an after trigger?
adderror after trigger rollback
What happens to DML done in a trigger when addError is called?
a: Yes. addError works on Trigger.new records in after insert and after update, and on Trigger.old in delete triggers. The record is saved but not yet committed, so calling addError makes that record's save fail. In an all-or-none operation the whole transaction rolls back, including any DML the trigger already did. With partial success, Salesforce rolls back and retries the save with only the good records. I use it in after triggers when the check depends on data that only exists after save. For example, if the rule counts records with a SOQL query and that count has to include the records being saved right now, the check has to run after save, because only then can the query see them. But for simple checks I prefer before triggers, because failing early avoids wasted work.
points: Works on Trigger.new in after insert/update and Trigger.old in delete
Record isn't committed yet, so it rolls back
Partial success: Salesforce retries with the good records
Prefer before triggers for simple validation

q: Write a trigger that handles undelete, and explain when it fires.
alt: When does an after undelete trigger run?
How do you handle records restored from the recycle bin in a trigger?
trigger after undelete example
Is Trigger.old available in undelete?
a: After undelete fires when records are restored from the Recycle Bin, either from the UI or with Database.undelete in Apex. There is only an after undelete event, and Trigger.new and Trigger.newMap hold the restored records, while Trigger.old is not available. A common use is recalculating a custom roll-up on the parent, because the restored child should count again. Here, when contacts are restored, I recount the contacts on their accounts with one aggregate query and one update.
points: Only after undelete exists
Trigger.new and newMap hold restored records
Typical use: recalculate custom roll-ups

q: How do you disable or bypass a trigger without deploying code?
alt: How do you switch off triggers during a data migration?
Trigger bypass using custom metadata or custom permission
how to bypass trigger for integration user
Can admins turn off a trigger in production without a deployment?
a: I give every trigger a kill switch. A custom metadata type, say Trigger_Setting__mdt, holds one record per object with an Is_Active__c checkbox, so an admin can switch an object's trigger logic off org-wide during a migration, and because it's metadata it can be deployed and is the same across environments. On top of that, a custom permission like Bypass_Triggers, given through a permission set to an integration or migration user, lets just that user skip the logic. The trigger checks both first, using getInstance and FeatureManagement.checkPermission, and getInstance doesn't use a SOQL query.
points: Custom metadata switch per object for org-wide disable
Custom permission via permission set for per-user bypass
FeatureManagement.checkPermission + Trigger_Setting__mdt.getInstance
No deployment needed to flip either switch

q: Can you write triggers on both standard and custom objects? Are there objects that don't support triggers?
alt: Can I write a trigger on a standard object like Account?
Which objects support Apex triggers?
trigger on custom object vs standard object
Can you write a trigger on a platform event?
a: Yes. Triggers work on custom objects and on most standard objects like Account, Contact, Opportunity, Case and Lead. They also work on some standard child objects, such as OpportunityLineItem, CaseComment and ContentVersion. A few standard objects don't support triggers, so I check the object reference before I plan the design. You can also write triggers on platform events and Change Data Capture change events, but those only support after insert. The syntax is the same; you just use the API name. For example, a trigger on Invoice__c for a custom object, or on Order_Event__e for a platform event. For Change Data Capture, the name ends in ChangeEvent, like AccountChangeEvent.
points: Custom objects and most standard objects support triggers
Some standard objects don't, check the object reference
Platform event and CDC triggers: after insert only
Use API names: __c, __e, ChangeEvent

q: If an Apex DML inserts 1,000 records, how many times does the trigger fire, and how do limits apply?
alt: What is the trigger batch size?
Does a trigger process records in chunks of 200?
1000 records inserted how many times trigger executes
Are governor limits reset between trigger chunks?
a: The trigger fires five times, once for each chunk of 200 records, and all five runs are in the same transaction. That means governor limits are shared, so if each run uses 30 queries, the fourth chunk will break the 100 SOQL limit. Static variables also carry over between chunks. With Data Loader it's different: each batch it sends, 200 records by default, is a separate API call and transaction, so limits apply per batch. This is why I keep the number of queries per trigger run constant and small, regardless of record count.
points: Trigger runs per chunk of 200 records
All chunks share one transaction and its limits
Static variables persist across chunks
Each Data Loader batch is its own transaction

q: Can you make a callout directly from a trigger?
alt: Why can't I call an external API from a trigger?
How do I make an HTTP callout from a trigger?
callout from triggers are currently not supported error
trigger callout future method or queueable
a: No. A synchronous callout isn't allowed from a trigger, because the trigger runs while the database transaction is open, and Salesforce won't hold it open while waiting on an external system. You get the error 'Callout from triggers are currently not supported'. The solution is to hand the work to asynchronous Apex: a future method marked callout=true, or preferably a Queueable that implements Database.AllowsCallouts. Say every new Account has to be sent to an ERP. The trigger collects the new Account Ids and enqueues one Queueable for the whole batch, not one per record, and that job makes the callout. The async job starts only after the transaction commits, so the external system only hears about data that was really saved.
points: Synchronous callouts are blocked in triggers
Use @future(callout=true) or Queueable with Database.AllowsCallouts
Async job runs after commit
Enqueue once per trigger run, not per record

q: How do you write a test class for a trigger?
alt: How do you test an Apex trigger?
Write a bulk test for a trigger
test class for trigger with 200 records
How do you get code coverage for a trigger?
a: I test the trigger through DML, because that's what fires it. I create my own test data with @TestSetup, never relying on org data, and I use 200 records to prove the trigger is bulk-safe. I put the DML between Test.startTest and Test.stopTest, so I get fresh limits and any async work finishes. Then I query the results and assert the actual outcome with the Assert class. For example, if the trigger defaults a Region on Accounts, I insert 200 Accounts, query them back, and assert all 200 got the right Region. I also cover negative paths, like asserting that addError blocks a bad record, and every event the trigger handles, not just insert.
points: Fire the trigger with DML on test data
Use 200 records to prove bulk safety
Test.startTest / stopTest, then assert results
Cover negative paths and all handled events

q: What happens to triggers when records are merged?
alt: Is there a merge trigger event?
How do you detect a merge in a delete trigger?
merge account trigger masterrecordid
Which triggers fire on a lead or contact merge?
a: A merge doesn't have its own trigger event; it fires delete and update events instead. The losing records fire before delete and after delete, and the winning record fires before update and after update. In the after delete trigger, the losing records in Trigger.old have MasterRecordId set to the winner's Id, so I check that field to tell a merge apart from a normal delete. Say two duplicate Accounts are merged. The duplicate shows up in after delete with MasterRecordId pointing at the survivor, so my code knows it's a merge, not someone really deleting a customer. Child records that get reparented to the winner during the merge don't fire their own triggers. That matters for custom roll-ups, so I recalculate for the master record myself.
points: No merge event: delete for losers, update for winner
MasterRecordId set on deleted losers in after delete
Reparented children don't fire triggers
Recalculate custom roll-ups for the winner

q: Your trigger fails with MIXED_DML_OPERATION. Why does it happen and how do you fix it?
alt: What is mixed DML error in Salesforce?
I update User and Account in the same trigger and get an error
mixed dml operation setup and non setup object
How do you avoid mixed DML in a test class?
a: MIXED_DML_OPERATION means the transaction did DML on a setup object, like User, Group, GroupMember or PermissionSetAssignment, and on a non-setup object like Account, in the same transaction. Salesforce blocks it because setup changes affect sharing and access calculations. A common case is a User trigger that fires when someone is deactivated and tries to reassign that person's Accounts in the same transaction. In a trigger, the fix is to move one side into a separate transaction, usually a Queueable or future method for the non-setup DML. In tests, I wrap the setup DML in System.runAs. Not every User update triggers it; it mostly appears when fields like role, profile, username or active status change.
points: Setup (User, Group, PermissionSetAssignment) + non-setup DML in one transaction
Fix: move one side to Queueable or future
Tests: use System.runAs around setup DML
Common trigger: user deactivation or role change

q: Are there operations that don't fire triggers?
alt: Which operations skip Apex triggers?
Does a cascade delete fire triggers on child records?
when do triggers not execute in salesforce
My trigger didn't run when records were deleted with the parent, why?
a: Yes, some system and mass operations skip triggers. Examples are cascading deletes of child records when a master record is deleted, child records reparented as part of a merge, mass campaign status changes, mass division transfers, mass address updates, renaming or replacing picklist values, changing a custom field's data type, and managing price books. So if my design depends on a trigger, I check whether one of these paths can bypass it. For example, say I keep a custom count of Contacts on Account using a Contact trigger. When two Accounts are merged, the Contacts moved to the winner don't fire that trigger, so the count goes stale. That's why I plan a recalculation, like a scheduled batch that reconciles the values.
points: Cascade deletes of children don't fire child triggers
Merge reparenting, mass updates, picklist renames skip triggers
Plan a reconciliation batch for critical roll-ups

q: How do triggers behave with partial-success DML like Database.insert with allOrNone set to false?
alt: Do triggers fire again when some records fail?
Database insert false trigger runs twice
What happens to static variables when Salesforce retries a partial save?
allornone false trigger retry behaviour
a: When some records fail, Salesforce rolls back that attempt and retries the save with only the records that succeeded, so the trigger fires again for them in the same transaction. Because it's the same transaction, static variables are not reset. That's a real trap. Say I update 100 records with allOrNone false and 5 fail. My trigger runs for all 100 and a recursion guard stores their Ids. The attempt is rolled back, the retry runs for the 95 good ones, and the guard says they're already done, so it skips them. The DML from the first attempt was rolled back, so the logic silently never happens. I keep guards tied to real field changes where possible, and I make sure counters and side effects can't be doubled or lost on a retry.
points: Failed attempt is rolled back, good records are retried
Trigger fires again in the same transaction
Static variables are NOT reset between attempts
Id-based guards can wrongly skip the retry

q: How would you design the trigger architecture for a large org with several teams working on the same objects?
alt: How do you organise triggers when many teams touch Account?
Design a scalable trigger framework for an enterprise org
metadata driven trigger framework
How do you stop teams overwriting each other's trigger logic?
a: I'd standardise on one trigger per object and a shared handler framework, so everyone plugs into the same entry point. Handlers stay thin and call service classes split by business domain. I'd use custom metadata to register and order handler classes, so a team adds logic without editing another team's code. For example, the sales team and the service team both need logic on Account. Each writes its own handler class and adds a metadata record with its run order, and nobody touches the other team's file. The framework provides one recursion approach, per-object and per-user bypass through custom metadata and custom permissions, and consistent error logging. I'd also agree when to use Flow versus Apex per object, require bulk tests with 200 records, and push heavy or callout work to Queueables.
points: One trigger per object, shared framework
Custom metadata registers and orders handlers per team
Common bypass, recursion and logging
Per-object Flow vs Apex standard, bulk tests mandatory

q: What is the scope of a static variable in a trigger?
alt: How long does a static variable live in Apex?
Are static variables shared between transactions?
static variable lifetime trigger context
Why do we use static variables in trigger handlers?
a: A static variable lives for the whole transaction, not just one trigger call. So if the same trigger runs several times in one transaction, because of 200-record chunks, a re-save from other automation, or a DML that fires it again, the static value is still there. That's why we use static variables for recursion guards and to cache query results within a transaction. For example, if my handler loads a map of region settings into a static variable during the first chunk, the next four chunks of a 1,000-record Apex insert reuse it instead of querying again. When the transaction ends, the value is gone and the next transaction starts fresh. Static variables are never shared between different users or different transactions.
points: Lives for one transaction
Persists across trigger chunks and re-fires
Used for recursion guards and caching
Not shared across transactions or users

q: How do you write a trigger on a platform event?
alt: Write a platform event subscriber trigger
Which events does a platform event trigger support?
platform event trigger after insert example
Which user does a platform event trigger run as?
a: A platform event trigger only supports after insert, because publishing an event is like inserting it. It runs asynchronously in its own transaction, and by default as the Automated Process user rather than the publisher, so I set owner fields explicitly if they matter. It can receive large batches, so I keep it bulk-safe. For resilience, I can use EventBus.TriggerContext setResumeCheckpoint, or throw EventBus.RetryableException, so events are retried instead of lost. For example, in my trigger on Order_Event__e, each event becomes an order log record. I build all the log records in one list and insert them once, however many events arrive in the batch.
points: Only after insert
Runs async, by default as Automated Process user
Bulk-safe: batches can be large
setResumeCheckpoint / RetryableException for resilience

q: What are the best practices for writing Apex triggers?
alt: Tell me trigger best practices
What rules do you follow when writing a trigger?
apex trigger best practices list
How do you write a good trigger?
a: The main ones: one trigger per object, with a thin trigger that calls a handler class. Bulkify everything, with no SOQL or DML inside loops, using Sets and Maps. Use before triggers for same-record updates and validation, and after triggers for related records. Only process records whose relevant fields changed, by comparing with oldMap. For example, if my logic reacts to an Opportunity's Stage, I skip records where someone only edited the Description. Prevent recursion with a static Set of Ids, not a Boolean. Never hard-code Ids. Move callouts and heavy work to Queueables. Add a bypass switch, and write bulk tests with 200 records.
points: One thin trigger per object + handler
Bulkify: no SOQL/DML in loops
Before for same record, after for related records
Check field changes, Id-based recursion guard, no hard-coded Ids
Async for callouts, bypass switch, bulk tests

q: How do you handle errors when your trigger updates related records?
alt: How do you show a friendly error when a related update fails in a trigger?
Database update with allOrNone false inside a trigger

q: Explain the order of execution in Salesforce when a record is saved.

a: When a record is saved, Salesforce loads the record and runs system validation, then runs before-save record-triggered flows, then before triggers. Next it re-runs system validation and custom validation rules, then duplicate rules. The record is saved to the database but not committed, and after triggers run. Then come assignment rules, auto-response rules, any remaining workflow rules, escalation rules, processes, and after-save record-triggered flows. After that, entitlement rules, roll-up summary updates on the parent and grandparent, and criteria-based sharing. Finally everything commits, and post-commit work runs, like sending emails and starting queued async jobs. Here's why it matters. If my before trigger sets a Case field and a validation rule checks that field, the rule sees my value, because validation runs after before triggers. But an email from that save only goes out once everything commits.

a: The CPU limit is 10 seconds synchronous, and it counts all Apex and declarative automation in the transaction, but not time spent in the database. I'd take a debug log, look at where the time goes, and put Limits.getCpuTime around the suspect sections. For example, if a trigger loops over 200 Opportunities and, for each one, loops over every line item in the batch to find its children, I replace that inner loop with a Map lookup and most of that work disappears. If the work is still heavy, I'd move the non-urgent part into a Queueable, which gets a 60 second CPU limit.
